extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and policymakers interested in national finance, trade, and public revenue (merchants, legislators, political economists)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methods for evaluating a nation's trade balance, public revenue, tax burden, and financial health, as argued in an 18th-century political-economy pamphlet. Emphasises how to interpret customs data, imports/exports, public debt, and prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs-entry inaccuracy limited to free goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The inaccuracy of these entries can extend only to FREE GOODS, that is, to such British products and manufactures, as are exported without drawback and without bounty; which do not in general amount to more than two thirds at the very utmost of the whole export even of our home products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize an observed over-entry error across all exports: the known error applies chiefly to free goods (exports without drawback/bounty) and therefore cannot by itself justify large downward adjustments of the whole balance of trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate (drawback) goods reliably recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: The article of CERTIFICATE GOODS re-exported, a vast branch of our commerce, admits of no error, (except some smaller frauds which cannot be estimated,) as they have all a drawback of duty, and the exporter must therefore correctly specify their quantity and kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing export data, treat certificate/drawback goods as accurately recorded and therefore reliable for measuring trade; exceptions are only small, estimable frauds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector-General accounts omit merchant/factory profits
rubrics_metrics.description: In the account made up at the Inspector-General's office, they estimate only the original cost of British products as they are here purchased; and on foreign goods, only the prices in the country from whence they are sent... the profits of the merchant at home, and of our factories abroad, are not taken into the account; which profit on such an immense quantity of goods exported and re-exported cannot fail of being very great: five per cent, upon the whole, I should think, a very moderate allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust customs-based export valuations upward to include merchant and factory profits (a modest blanket allowance such as ~5% is proposed) because official entries record only original cost/prices in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include value of shipping services paid by foreigners
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not comprehend the advantage arising from the employment of 600,000 tons of shipping, which must be paid by the foreign consumer, and which, in many bulky articles of commerce, is equal to the value of the commodity. This can scarcely be rated at less than a million annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for transportation/shipping costs (paid by foreign buyers) as part of the export advantage — shipping capacity and freight translate into national gain and should be added to trade value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat imperial/colonial imports as domestic profit (don't net them off)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole import from Ireland and America, and from the West Indies, is set against us in the ordinary way of striking a balance of imports and exports; whereas the import and export are both our own. The whole revolves and circulates through this kingdom, and is, so far as regards our profit, in the nature of home trade...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically set colonial/imperial imports against national exports when measuring national advantage; where both sides of the trade accrue to the same polity, treat such flows as largely domestic circulation and count their net profit as internal benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure Newfoundland trade by foreign sale, not import entries
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom-house entries furnish a most defective, and, indeed, ridiculous idea of the most valuable branch of trade we have in the world,--that with Newfoundland. ... The vessels in that trade go straight from Newfoundland to the foreign market; and the sale there, not the import here, is the measure of its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For trades where goods are shipped onward from a colony to third-country markets, value should be measured by the proceeds of those foreign sales rather than by domestic import entries, which understate the branch's true importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider quality/nature of imports (raw materials vs luxury)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of your imports must be considered as well as the quantity. To state the whole of the foreign import as loss, is exceedingly absurd. All the iron, hemp, flax, cotton, Spanish wool, raw silk, woollen and linen-yarn, which we import, are by no means to be considered as the matter of a merely luxurious consumption; which are materials of industry, not of luxury, which are wrought up here, in many instances, to ten times, and more, of their original value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish imports that are raw materials (which enable domestic manufacture and high value-added) from imports of luxury consumption; raw-material imports should be treated as contributions to internal wealth rather than mere losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use averages, not accidents, when judging price levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Take average and not accident, the grand and first necessary of life is cheap in this country; and that too as weighed, not against labor, which is its true counterpoise, but against money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prices by long-run averages rather than short-term accidents; evaluate the cost of necessities relative to labor (wages) and money supply rather than in nominal terms alone to avoid misleading conclusions about affordability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare prices of necessities relative to labor and money supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Does he call the price of wheat at this day, between 32 and 40 shillings per quarter in London dear? ... Diminish the [money supply], and meat in your markets will be sufficiently cheap in account, but much dearer in effect: because fewer will be in a condition to buy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether food is 'dear' or 'cheap', consider wages and purchasing power — reductions in money supply may lower nominal prices but worsen real affordability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three standards for judging a nation's financial condition
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three standards to judge of the good condition of a nation with regard to its finances. 1st, The relief of the people. 2nd, The equality of supplies to establishments. 3rd, The state of public credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate national fiscal health along these three axes: (1) Whether taxation provides relief/proportional fairness to the people; (2) Whether supplies/revenues are adequate and equitably matched to government establishments/expenses; (3) The condition of public credit (market confidence and fund prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest burden as an indicator of comparative fiscal health
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest paid by France, funded and unfunded, ... after the tax of 10 per cent                £6,500,000; Interest paid by England, as stated by the author, p. 27                            4,600,000 ... Interest paid by France exceeds that paid by England £1,900,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the absolute and relative interest payments on public debt between countries: heavier interest burdens indicate worse fiscal strain even if nominal debt levels differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market prices of government funds to judge public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the reader cast his eye on a table of the price of French funds... compared with the state of some of our English stocks... This state of the funds of France and England is sufficient to convince even prejudice and obstinacy, that if France and England are not in the same condition ... the difference is infinitely to the disadvantage of France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect government fund/stock prices as empirical indicators of national creditworthiness and investor confidence; depressed prices signal weak public credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess taxes by burden, administration, and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Her subjects pay more than England, on a computation of the wealth of both countries; that her taxes are more injudiciously and more oppressively imposed; more vexatiously collected; come in a smaller proportion to the royal coffers, and are less applied by far to the public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing tax systems, consider: tax burden relative to national wealth, fairness of imposition, burdensome collection methods, revenue yield to the treasury, and efficiency/appropriateness of expenditure of proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming facts to support a theory; base claims on probability and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In general this author is so circumstanced, that to support his theory he is obliged to assume his facts: and then, if you allow his facts, they will not support his conclusions. ... In speaking of a foreign revenue, the very pretence to accuracy would be the most inaccurate thing in the world. Neither the author nor I can with certainty authenticate the information we communicate to the public, nor in an affair of eternal fluctuation arrive at perfect exactness. All we can do, and this we may be expected to do, is to avoid gross errors and blunders of a capital nature. We cannot order the proper officer to lay the accounts before the House. But the reader must judge on the probability of the accounts we lay before him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not predicate large conclusions on assumed or unverified facts; aim to avoid gross errors, state uncertainties, and judge accounts by their probability given accessible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base reform estimates on existing establishments and justify deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: One would have thought the natural method in a plan of reformation would be, to take the present existing estimates as they stand; and then to show what may be practicably and safely defalcated from them. ... Hardly a word on any of these points, the only points however that are in the least essential; for unless you assign reasons for the increase or diminution of the several articles of public charge, the playing at establishments and estimates is an amusement of no higher order...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In proposing changes to public establishments or budgets, start from current, concrete estimates and explicitly justify each proposed reduction or increase; avoid speculative 'play' with figures ungrounded in existing accounts.
